questions.stem: Six hours after a first dose of IM haloperidol for agitation, a 22-year-old client's head is twisted to one side, the eyes are rolled upward and the client is drooling and has trouble swallowing. The client is alert and frightened. Temperature is 37.1 °C (98.8 °F). Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Give IM or IV diphenhydramine or benztropine as prescribed
Stay with the client and watch the airway closely
Give another dose of haloperidol to calm the client
Apply cold packs to the neck muscles and wait
Restrain the client's head to straighten the neck

parameters.text: Body weight measured once a week

rationale.correct: Acute dystonia occurs hours to days after starting antipsychotics, especially high-potency ones in young men; treat with anticholinergics and protect the airway.

perOption.c1: Sudden painful spasms of the neck, eyes and throat after a first dose of a high-potency antipsychotic are acute dystonia.
perOption.c2: NMS causes high fever, rigidity and confusion; the client is alert and afebrile.
perOption.c3: Tardive dyskinesia develops after long-term use.
perOption.c4: Sustained twisting postures after haloperidol point to dystonia.
perOption.a2: Spasm of the throat muscles can threaten the airway.
perOption.a5: Forcing the neck can injure the client.
perOption.p1: Laryngeal dystonia is the dangerous form.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: A client with diabetic ketoacidosis has received 2 L of saline. Before the insulin infusion starts, the nurse sees new labs: glucose 486 mg/dL, pH 7.14 and potassium 3.0 mEq/L. The ECG shows flattened T waves and U waves, and the client reports leg weakness. Complete the diagram by placing the condition that poses the most immediate threat, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Hold the insulin infusion and notify the provider
Give IV potassium replacement as prescribed by pump
Start the insulin infusion right away as planned
Give potassium by IV push to raise it faster
Give sodium bicarbonate to correct the pH first

parameters.text: Body weight measured once a week
Pupil size and reaction to light
Bowel sounds in each of the four quadrants

rationale.correct: In DKA, check potassium before insulin: if below 3.3 mEq/L, hold insulin and replace potassium first, with cardiac monitoring.

perOption.c1: Insulin moves potassium into cells; starting it with a potassium below 3.3 can cause dangerous dysrhythmias.
perOption.a1: Insulin is held until potassium is at least 3.3 mEq/L.
perOption.a5: Bicarbonate lowers potassium further and is reserved for very low pH.
perOption.p1: Guides when insulin can be started.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
American Diabetes Association Standards of Care
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize low potassium before insulin in DKA.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old client who weighs 76 kg with diabetic ketoacidosis and a potassium of 4.2 mEq/L is to start a regular insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hr. The pharmacy supplies regular insulin 100 units in 100 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride. At what rate should the nurse set the pump? Round to one decimal place.

rationale.correct: Dose: 0.1 units x 76 kg = 7.6 units/hr. Concentration: 100 units / 100 mL = 1 unit/mL. Rate: 7.6 mL/hr.

questions.stem: At follow-up visits in a primary care clinic, the nurse reviews four clients who started new medications 3 months ago and is evaluating whether each medication is working. For each medication, indicate the finding that best shows a therapeutic effect.

columns.text: Weight down 2 kg and less ankle swelling
More energy and a normal TSH
Lower serum uric acid and no gout attacks

rationale.correct: Evaluate each drug by its intended effect: diuretics by weight and edema, levothyroxine by TSH and symptoms, allopurinol by uric acid and metformin by A1C.

perOption.r2:c2: Normal thyroid levels and energy show effect.
perOption.r3:c3: Lower uric acid and no attacks show effect.
perOption.r4:c4: A lower A1C shows better glucose control.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to give a unit of packed red blood cells. Which actions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use a large-gauge IV catheter, such as 18 to 20 gauge, for an adult
Prime the tubing with 0.9% sodium chloride
Start the transfusion within 30 minutes of getting the blood from the blood bank
Hang the blood with a bag of 5% dextrose in water as the primary fluid
Take baseline vital signs before starting
Complete the unit within 4 hours

rationale.correct: Transfusion: large-gauge IV, saline only, start within 30 minutes, baseline vital signs, close watch early and finish within 4 hours.

perOption.a: Prevents damage to cells and allows good flow.
perOption.b: Saline is the only solution compatible with blood.
perOption.c: Limits bacterial growth and cell breakdown.
perOption.d: Dextrose causes red cells to clump and break down.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: The nurse is giving a subcutaneous dose of heparin 5,000 units. Place the steps in order.

items.text: Inject slowly, remove the needle and do not rub the site
Clean the site on the abdomen at least 5 cm from the navel
Pinch the skin and insert the needle at a 90-degree angle
Identify the client with two identifiers and check the dose

rationale.correct: Subcutaneous heparin: identify, check, clean a site away from the navel, insert at 45 to 90 degrees, inject slowly and do not rub.

questions.stem: A client has taken phenytoin for 2 years. Which teaching point addresses a common long-term adverse effect?

options.text: Avoid dairy foods such as milk and yogurt while taking phenytoin
Brush, floss and see a dentist regularly
Expect hair loss on the scalp over the next few years
Stop the drug if the gums become sore

rationale.correct: Phenytoin long-term effects: gingival hyperplasia, excess hair growth and bone loss; teach oral care and never stop suddenly.

perOption.b: Phenytoin often causes gum overgrowth; good oral care helps.
perOption.c: Phenytoin is more likely to cause excess body hair.

questions.stem: Three days after stopping paroxetine 40 mg on their own because they felt better, a client reports dizziness, "electric shock" feelings in the head, irritability, nausea and vivid dreams. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: A return of the client's depression after stopping treatment
SSRI discontinuation syndrome after a sudden stop
Serotonin syndrome from a new interaction
An inner ear infection causing vertigo

rationale.correct: SSRIs, especially paroxetine, should be tapered; stopping suddenly causes discontinuation symptoms.

perOption.a: Relapse usually develops over weeks and does not cause electric-shock feelings.
perOption.b: Stopping a short-acting SSRI suddenly causes dizziness, electric-shock sensations, irritability and nausea.
perOption.c: Serotonin syndrome comes from too much serotonin, not stopping a drug.
perOption.d: The timing and the electric-shock feelings point to discontinuation.

questions.stem: For each medication, choose the correct injection technique.

cells.text: Insulin in an adult with normal body fat

options.text: Intradermal at a 10- to 15-degree angle
Intramuscular at 90 degrees
Subcutaneous at 45 degrees
Subcutaneous at 45 degrees
Z-track into a large muscle
Intradermal at 15 degrees
Subcutaneous at 90 degrees
Intramuscular at 90 degrees
Intradermal at 10 degrees

rationale.correct: Injection techniques: intradermal 10 to 15 degrees, subcutaneous 45 to 90 degrees, IM 90 degrees, and Z-track for irritating drugs.

perOption.b2:a: Iron dextran is given deep IM.
perOption.b2:b: Z-track prevents leakage and skin staining.
perOption.b3:a: Subcutaneous with a short pen needle at 90 degrees.
perOption.b3:b: Insulin is not given IM routinely.

questions.stem: A client who takes clonidine 0.2 mg twice daily for hypertension is NPO for surgery and missed the last two doses. The client now has a headache, is anxious and sweating and has a blood pressure of 204/112 mm Hg. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Expected anxiety before surgery
Rebound hypertension from the missed clonidine
An allergic reaction to the chlorhexidine surgical skin prep
Low blood sugar from fasting before surgery

rationale.correct: Clonidine and beta-blockers must not be stopped suddenly; missed doses can cause rebound hypertension and tachycardia.

perOption.a: Anxiety does not usually raise blood pressure this much.
perOption.b: Stopping clonidine suddenly can cause a dangerous rise in blood pressure; the provider must be notified.
perOption.c: Allergy does not cause this picture.
perOption.d: Hypoglycemia causes sweating but not severe hypertension.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client taking aspirin 81 mg and clopidogrel after a coronary stent asks about pain relief for a sprained ankle. Which response is best?

options.text: "Ibuprofen is fine for a few days."
"Use acetaminophen and ice, not ibuprofen."
"Stop the clopidogrel until the ankle has fully healed."
"Double the aspirin for a few days for pain."

rationale.correct: Clients on antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy should avoid NSAIDs; acetaminophen is preferred for pain.

perOption.a: NSAIDs add to bleeding risk with antiplatelet drugs.
perOption.b: Acetaminophen does not add bleeding risk; NSAIDs raise the risk of GI bleeding with antiplatelets.
perOption.c: Stopping antiplatelets after a stent risks stent thrombosis.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach safe pain relief with antiplatelet therapy.

questions.stem: A client with sepsis from a leg wound has a record listing a penicillin allergy with anaphylaxis and throat swelling at age 20. Highlight the prescriptions the nurse should question before giving.

rationale.correct: Question any penicillin-class drug for a client with a penicillin allergy, especially anaphylaxis; check cephalosporins with the provider.

perOption.r3: A macrolide; no cross-reactivity with penicillin.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client has heavy bleeding 30 minutes after birth with a boggy uterus. The provider prescribes methylergonovine 0.2 mg IM. The client's blood pressure is 158/104 mm Hg, and the client was treated for preeclampsia. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the methylergonovine as prescribed, since bleeding is the priority
Hold it, keep massaging and ask the provider for another drug
Give half the dose and recheck the blood pressure in 15 minutes
Give the dose orally instead of IM so that it has a milder effect on blood pressure

rationale.correct: Methylergonovine is contraindicated with hypertension and preeclampsia; alternatives include oxytocin, carboprost (not with asthma) and misoprostol.

perOption.a: Methylergonovine raises blood pressure and is contraindicated in hypertension and preeclampsia.
perOption.b: Other uterotonics, such as carboprost if no asthma, can be used; massage continues.
perOption.c: Changing the dose does not remove the risk.
perOption.d: The route does not remove the contraindication.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client recovering from acute pancreatitis is starting oral intake. Which meal is most appropriate?

options.text: A cheeseburger with fries and a milkshake
Broth, plain rice and baked chicken
A large bowl of creamy soup with buttered bread on the side
Fried eggs, bacon and whole milk

rationale.correct: After pancreatitis, start with small, low-fat meals and avoid alcohol.

perOption.b: Low-fat, small meals are better tolerated as the pancreas recovers.
perOption.c: Cream and butter are high in fat.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for four clients on a surgical step-down unit after different procedures. For each client, indicate the most appropriate position.

rows.text: A client 2 hours after a craniotomy
A client after a cardiac catheterization through the femoral artery
A client receiving a cleansing enema

columns.text: Head of bed at 30 degrees, head midline
Flat with the affected leg straight

rationale.correct: Positioning: head up 30 degrees and midline after craniotomy, leg straight after femoral catheterization, semi-Fowler's with neck support after thyroidectomy and left side-lying for enemas.

perOption.r1:c1: Elevation with a midline head supports venous drainage and lowers ICP.
perOption.r2:c2: Keeps the femoral site still to prevent bleeding.
perOption.r3:c3: Semi-Fowler's with neck support reduces swelling and strain on the incision.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client with bone metastases has needed higher doses of morphine over 3 months for the same pain relief. The client's spouse worries the client is "becoming an addict." How should the nurse explain this?

options.text: "The client is addicted and should be weaned off morphine."
"This is tolerance; addiction means craving and harmful use."
"The cancer must be spreading because the morphine is working less well."
"The morphine will soon stop working completely."

rationale.correct: Tolerance (needing more for the same effect) and physical dependence are expected with long-term opioids; addiction is compulsive use despite harm.

perOption.a: Needing higher doses for the same effect is tolerance, not addiction.
perOption.b: Tolerance is a physical adaptation and does not mean addiction.
perOption.c: Tolerance can occur without disease progression, though progression is also assessed.
perOption.d: Doses can be adjusted or drugs rotated.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client in the intensive care unit has slept poorly for 3 nights. Which interventions should the nurse use to promote sleep? Select all that apply.

options.text: Dim the lights and close the door at night when it is safe
Cluster care so the client has 90-minute periods without interruption
Keep the television on all night for company
Offer earplugs and an eye mask
Open the blinds in the morning to let in daylight
Give a sedative-hypnotic every night as the first step

rationale.correct: Promote ICU sleep with lighting and noise control, clustered care, earplugs and eye masks and daylight exposure.

perOption.f: Drugs are not the first measure and can cause delirium.

questions.stem: A client receiving chemotherapy has painful mouth sores. Which oral care instruction is most appropriate?

options.text: Rinse with an alcohol-based mouthwash after each meal
Use a soft toothbrush and rinse often with saline
Brush firmly with a hard toothbrush to remove plaque
Eat spicy foods to stimulate the flow of saliva

rationale.correct: Mucositis care: soft brush, frequent saline or baking soda rinses, no alcohol mouthwash and bland, soft foods.

perOption.a: Alcohol dries and irritates the mucosa.
perOption.b: Gentle cleaning and bland rinses keep the mouth clean without injury.

questions.stem: A client had a cast applied to the left forearm 6 hours ago. Highlight the findings that need immediate follow-up.

segments.text: pain that is getting worse despite the prescribed oxycodone
pale and cool, with capillary refill of 4 seconds
The cast is dry on the outside
The arm is raised on a pillow

rationale.correct: Neurovascular warning signs after casting: increasing pain, pallor, coolness, slow capillary refill, numbness and tingling.

perOption.s2: Increasing pain despite analgesia can signal compartment syndrome.
perOption.s6: Nerve compression is a warning sign.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A resident with moderate dementia in long-term care has frequent urinary incontinence but can walk to the bathroom with cues. Which intervention is most appropriate?

options.text: Insert an indwelling catheter to keep the skin dry
Prompt and help the resident to the toilet on a schedule
Limit fluids after lunch so the resident voids less
Use adult briefs and change them twice a day at set times

rationale.correct: Prompted voiding on a schedule helps residents with dementia stay continent.

perOption.a: Catheters raise infection risk and are not used for incontinence alone.
perOption.b: Prompted voiding reduces incontinence in residents with dementia.
perOption.c: Fluid restriction causes dehydration and concentrated urine.
perOption.d: Infrequent changes harm skin and do not address the cause.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A 71-year-old client with Parkinson's disease often "freezes" when trying to walk through a doorway at home. Which technique should the nurse teach?

options.text: Lean forward and walk faster to get through the doorway
Stop, stand tall, then step over an imagined line on the floor
Shuffle the feet close to the floor to keep balance
Turn around and walk backward slowly through the doorway

rationale.correct: For freezing in Parkinson's disease, use cues such as stepping over a line, counting or music.

perOption.b: Visual and rhythmic cues help overcome freezing.
perOption.c: Shuffling is part of the problem.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client with a new colostomy. Complete the sentences.

content.template: A healthy stoma should look {{b1}}. If the stoma turns {{b2}}, the client should call right away. The opening of the pouch should be about {{b3}}.

options.text: moist and pink to red
dry and pale
dark purple
dark purple or black
slightly swollen in the first weeks
bright red after cleaning
about 3 mm (1/8 in) larger than the stoma
much larger than the stoma to allow air
the same size or smaller than the stoma

rationale.correct: A healthy stoma is moist and red; a dusky or black stoma needs urgent reporting; the pouch opening is cut about 3 mm larger than the stoma.

perOption.b1:a: A healthy stoma is moist and red.
perOption.b1:b: This suggests poor blood flow or dehydration.
perOption.b2:a: This means the stoma is losing its blood supply.
perOption.b3:a: This protects the skin without squeezing the stoma.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client is prescribed knee-high graduated compression stockings. When should the nurse apply them?

options.text: In the morning before the client gets out of bed
At bedtime, so they work while the client sleeps
After the client has walked for an hour
Once the ankles look swollen later in the day

rationale.correct: Apply compression stockings in the morning before the client gets up, smooth out wrinkles and remove them daily to check the skin.

perOption.a: Applying them before the legs swell gives the best fit and effect.
perOption.b: They are applied in the morning before swelling develops.
perOption.c: By then the legs may already be swollen.
perOption.d: They are used to prevent swelling.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: A client tells the nurse they have lost their savings betting online and keep going back to win it back. Which response is best?

options.text: "Just stop betting. It's that simple."
"This seems hard to control. Would you like help with treatment?"
"Everyone gambles sometimes, so don't worry about it."
"Try betting smaller amounts so that you lose less money each week."

rationale.correct: Gambling disorder is a behavioral addiction; acknowledge it, assess for suicide risk and refer to treatment and support groups.

perOption.a: Gambling disorder is not overcome by willpower alone.
perOption.b: Acknowledging the problem and offering referral supports change.
perOption.d: This does not address the disorder.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: A client with schizophrenia whose hallucinations are controlled spends most of the day in bed, rarely showers and shows little interest in activities. Which intervention best addresses these symptoms?

options.text: Tell the client they need to join each group or they will lose privileges
Set small daily goals, such as showering, and praise progress
Increase the antipsychotic dose until the symptoms stop
Let the client stay in bed, since rest is part of recovery

rationale.correct: Negative symptoms (avolition, anhedonia, flat affect) improve with structured routines, small goals and reinforcement.

perOption.a: Punitive approaches do not help negative symptoms.
perOption.b: Negative symptoms such as avolition respond to small, achievable goals and positive reinforcement.
perOption.c: Higher doses rarely improve negative symptoms and add side effects.
